judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: Neat 'Oh, this is terrible! Terrible!' opener and a clean plea / found / follow / thanks arc, but it follows the same beat sheet as B, E, I and J, down to 'Please, kind sir, bring him home'.

items.label: B
items.critique: Parent-loses-child-to-curiosity premise and 'Oh, my boy! You're safe!' match A and I closely; 'May all that is great bless you!' is a nice touch but the shape is templated.

items.label: C
items.critique: Specific mechanical plot (express elevator jammed, gears, a key to circle back to the gate, a secret passage), awkward 'We best go' and 'You'll make a fine [Group], lad' are the original's mission-briefing register.

items.label: D
items.critique: 'Hail, brave Adventurer! We are innocent victims...' and 'the menfolk ... cannot live without us!' carry Westwood's tongue-in-cheek humour and slightly clumsy punctuation.

items.label: E
items.critique: 'You great oaf, you're alive!' and the hot bowl at the inn are warm but over-crafted; 'I can hear them rattling!' and 'before they come back' recur across the new rescue texts.

items.label: F
items.critique: Long multi-page briefing with a key, a scroll, 'Nox's vital interests', a count in the journal ('Rescue the 6 trapped mine workers') and a captain handoff: Westwood's practical, slightly bureaucratic quest shape.

items.label: G
items.critique: The frog in the burning house, 'Anything you find in that room you may keep!' and the 'Loads and loads of money?' joke are unmistakably Nox.

items.label: H
items.critique: Very terse lines ('Help us!'), 'before the Ogres eat them!' and 'go find the other two groups of damsels' fit Westwood's blunt, slightly comic campaign dialogue.

items.label: I
items.critique: Same parent-and-son template ('My boy! You're safe! Oh, thank you, thank you') with an over-explained setup ('I'm too old to fight, and nobody else will go'); the two-name journal is careful but generic.

items.label: J
items.critique: 'The boy has the brains of a goose, may the heavens forgive me' is an added flourish; 'Did [Person] send you?' and 'Hurry! I think they're coming back!' repeat other new texts almost word for word.

tells: The new rescue texts all follow one family drama (a parent or master's boy wanders off out of curiosity or is dragged off), with the same lines in each slot: 'Please, kind sir, bring him home', 'Please, hurry!', 'Did X send you?', 'I think they're coming back!', '[Person]! You're safe!'.
Westwood's rescues are tied to campaign mechanics: elevators, keys, scrolls, a count of captives, a handoff to the next NPC or mission; the new ones end with a small personal gift and a blessing.
Westwood's captive lines are often curt or flat ('I'll follow you.', 'Help us!'); the new ones are evenly emotive and polished.

Westwood's humour is broad and situational (menfolk who cannot live without the maidens, 'Loads and loads of money?'); the new texts' humour is a small character aside ('brains of a goose', 'You great oaf').
